planting.note: Set out container-grown divisions in spring in deep, humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in part to full shade; this creeping Japanese woodland sage slowly colonizes an area through trailing stems and benefits from a loose leaf-litter mulch that mimics its native forest floor.

directions: Unlike most sun-loving salvias, this understory species from Japanese forests is genuinely shade tolerant and even performs in deep shade where little else flowers. Soft, pale yellow, two-lipped blooms appear on upright spikes above the trailing foliage in late summer and early fall, a season when most woodland perennials have already finished. The lax, spreading stems root as they travel, so it works well as a loose groundcover beneath deciduous trees rather than as a tidy clump. Keep the soil consistently moist and rich in leaf mold, since it struggles in dry shade.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade; this low Japanese sage was collected by plantsman Barry Yinger and is grown chiefly for its white-edged foliage rather than its flowers.

directions: This dwarf woodland sage forms a low mound of crinkled green leaves edged in creamy white, a variegation pattern that stays crisp in the cool shade of a woodland bed but can wash out in hot afternoon sun. Short spikes of soft creamy-yellow flowers appear in mid to late summer, though gardeners mainly grow it for the foliage contrast against darker shade companions like hostas and ferns. Give it steady moisture and rich organic soil, since it does not tolerate drying out between waterings the way many sun-loving salvias do. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade; this compact Japanese sage spreads gradually into a tidy mound and resents hot, dry sites.

directions: Named for its two-tone pink flowers, which translate roughly as peach blossom, this Japanese woodland sage blooms late in the season from September into October when most other shade perennials have already gone dormant for the year. Its mounded habit and glossy, toothed foliage make it a useful shade groundcover that stays tidy without spreading aggressively. It is notably resistant to deer and rabbit browsing, a useful trait for woodland gardens bordering wild areas. Keep soil evenly moist through summer heat, since it will not tolerate prolonged dry spells in deep shade.

planting.note: Start seed indoors or set out container plants after the soil warms in average, well-drained soil in part sun to part shade; Balkan sage self-sows modestly where happy and appreciates some afternoon shade in hot-summer climates.

directions: Native to woodland margins in the Balkans and Caucasus, this sage carries tall spikes of pale yellow flowers marked with maroon-purple streaks on the lower lip, a striking combination that blooms from summer into early autumn. It is more tolerant of part shade than most border salvias and holds up well under the dappled light at the edge of a tree canopy. The coarse, heart-shaped basal leaves form a modest rosette before the flowering stems rise well above the foliage. Deadhead spent spikes to extend bloom and limit self-sowing in beds where volunteers are not wanted.

planting.note: Start seed indoors or set out container plants after the soil warms in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; this clump-forming sage is more forgiving of light afternoon shade than most Salvia nemorosa types.

directions: This Romanian native produces dense, narrow spikes of small lavender-blue flowers from early summer well into September, giving a long season of bloom relative to its compact size. Bees and butterflies visit the flowers heavily, and the wiry stems hold up without flopping even in looser soil. It tolerates part shade better than many border sages, making it a useful edging plant where a bed gets only half a day of sun. Cut plants back hard after the first flush to encourage a second round of bloom in late summer.
